title: A.G. Sulzberger: Seek the Facts, Even Those You Disagree With
summary: The New York Times publisher spoke with Melissa Bell, C.E.O. of Chicago Public Media, at the University of Chicago’s Institute of Politics on Nov. 10.
body_markdown:
The New York Times publisher spoke with Melissa Bell, C.E.O. of Chicago Public Media, at the University of Chicago’s Institute of Politics on Nov. 10.


On the most contested issues, tech platforms serve the American public with messages designed to stoke outrage and fear, A.G. Sulzberger told students at the University of Chicago.


“The incentive structure of the big tech companies … is not necessarily aligned with the best interests of society,” he said. “It’s aligned with the best interests of engagement.”


Journalists who go to the scene of the story and who follow professional processes and standards that ensure the accuracy of their reporting are the ones who provide the public with the full story.


“Whether it’s abortion rights or Israel-Palestine or trans rights or immigration, you actually want the full story,” Sulzberger said. “You want to be fully armed with the facts, either to challenge your thinking or just as likely, so you can argue your point and win the day more effectively. And I think independent news organizations are built to serve those people who are willing to be challenged, not with just what they want to be true, but the thing that may make them a little uncomfortable, but at the end of the day, be just as useful.”


At The New York Times, Sulzberger said, “we do not let outside forces influence our journalism. Our journalism should be independent. That is the word that I repeat more than any other in my job.”


The best way to stay informed on important issues is to find a news organization — “it doesn’t have to be the Times,” he said, “but a news organization that is doing independent, original work that is worthy of your trust.”
